Marcus to schedule a 2-week pilot and benchmark window (proposed start 2025-10-20)
Cobalt to provide a sample 1k qps traffic trace and list of compliance requirements

transcript:
Meeting header...

[00:00] Aisha Patel (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. It's 4pm PT, uh October 9th. We have about an hour allocated, looks like. Thanks Rajiv, Sofia, Tom for making time.
[00:18] Rajiv Menon (Cobalt CTO): Yeah thanks Aisha. We're excited to dig into the... the burst strategy and how this would run across our VPC and on-prem cluster. Just quick context: we're regulated medtech, so data residency and audit trails are big.
[00:35] Marcus Li (Redwood SE): Awesome, thanks Rajiv. Quick intro from me — Marcus, SE, I focus on serving runtime and autoscaling. Today I'd like to cover queueing models, warm pools, KV cache warmup, and tradeoffs for reserved GPUs vs hosted burst. We'll also talk about circuit breaker and fallback models.
[00:52] Sofia Alvarez (Head of ML Infra): Great. We have a hybrid setup: core inference in our on‑prem datacenter (NVIDIA A100s) for PHI workloads and a cloud VPC for non-PHI. We want to understand if Redwood can route burst traffic to hosted while keeping PHI on-prem, plus how we set burst thresholds.
[01:10] Tom Becker (SRE): Also interested in tail latency — our SLAs are 95th < 180ms for short completion tasks and cost needs to be predictable.
[01:25] Aisha: Perfect. First quick question: do you currently have any reserved GPU commitments? It helps frame sizing and burst headroom.
[01:32] Rajiv: We have a small reserved pool on-prem (6 A100s) and 8 on cloud through our cloud partner, but the cloud instances can't process PHI due to our policy.
[01:43] Marcus: OK, so requirement summary I'm hearing: PHI stays on-prem, non-PHI can be routed to hosted; need predictable cost and 95th tail targets; want autoscaling with burst to hosted for non-PHI. Is that accurate?
[01:58] Rajiv: Yes.

[02:10] Marcus: Let's jump into a simple queueing model. At heart we have arrival rate lambda and service rate mu per GPU. For A100s with your typical L2-7 transformer (seq len 512) our benchmark mu is about 6 requests/sec per GPU when running mixed precision FP16 with quantization off; with int8/QLoRA-like quant it's higher. But the important bit is how you provision headroom for peaks.
[02:35] Sofia: Sorry can you slow — you said 6 rps per GPU? That feels low; our per-request token count is usually small — 40 tokens on average, maybe 80.
[02:44] Marcus: Right — for 40 tokens the throughput is higher, around 12 rps. The numbers vary with sequence length, model size, and beam/temperature. The spreadsheet I'll send has a per‑model per‑sequence profile matrix.
[03:02] Tom: The spreadsheet link please.
[03:06] Aisha: We'll drop the benchmark sheet in the followups — it's linked in the notes. Quick note on KV cache: if you have session affinity and reuse, effective mu improves dramatically because KV cache avoids recompute on prefix tokens.
[03:20] Rajiv: Our use case is conversational triage; clients open sessions that last minutes to hours and many requests reuse context. So KV caching sounds useful.
[03:30] Marcus: Exactly — with warm KV cache hit rates > 70% you'll see tail latency improvements and higher throughput per GPU. The caveat is cache warming during burst: if requests get routed to hosted cold there will be an initial tail spike.
[03:45] Sofia: Can we pre-warm hosted nodes for known heavy sessions? Like a warm pool that maintains KV for certain user cohorts?
[03:52] Marcus: Yes. Redwood supports warm pools and pre-warm APIs. For privacy, you'd want to send only non-PHI context to hosted and maintain PHI-only session state on-prem. We can pre-warm model weights and KV prefixes that are safe to share — e.g., public system prompts, templates, or domain tokens that don't contain PHI.
[04:10] Rajiv: Ok makes sense. How does the autoscaler decide when to spillover to hosted? Is it queue length, latency SLO breach, or utilization?
[04:22] Marcus: You can configure policies: threshold-based (GPU utilization > x%), queue length (> y requests waiting), or latency SLO (95th > target). Most customers use a hybrid policy: primary trigger is queue length/queued_ms to avoid saturating GPU compute, with utilization as secondary.
[04:39] Aisha: We also offer predictive bursting — using short-term load forecasts to pre-provision burst capacity to reduce cold-starts.
[04:48] Sofia: How do you forecast? Is it ML-based or simple moving averages?
[04:52] Marcus: A mix — short-term autoregressive models plus heuristics, with a conservative margin. But customers with strict cost constraints prefer explicit warm pool rules tied to expected schedules (e.g., morning batches) rather than probabilistic forecast.

[05:10] Tom: Suppose we have a 2x expected spike for 5-10 minutes; what's the recommended reserved buffer? And what's the expected cost delta if we shift to hosted for that window?
[05:20] Marcus: For short spikes under 10 minutes, we recommend a small warm buffer of 10-20% reserved GPUs plus burst-to-hosted. Cost impact depends on hosted tier pricing; the sizing sheet will show token-cost and GPU-hour cost. Quick back-of-envelope: one A100-hour of hosted at peak provisioning to cover a 2x spike could cost a few hundred dollars — but amortized over the spike it might be cheaper than permanently reserving extra capacity on-prem.
[05:47] Rajiv: For compliance, we can't send PHI to hosted. But could we run a mixed strategy where request-level routing is based on a tagging field? e.g., any payload with PHI flag stays on-prem and other requests route out.
[05:59] Marcus: Yes — Redwood supports per-request routing metadata (customer tags) and policy-based routing in the control plane. You can enforce that PHI stays on-prem at the ingress layer. We also have query-level redaction integrations if you want to scrub identifiers before sending to hosted.
[06:15] Sofia: That's good. About KV cache again: when we have session affinity on-prem and we burst to hosted, do you replicate KV across environments or have a fallback to murkier behavior?
[06:26] Marcus: We don't replicate PHI KV across environments automatically. For non-PHI KV, you can choose to sync prefixes via an encrypted channel. More typical is to allow hosted to build KV from the subsequent user requests (cold) while on-prem sessions continue to use their local cache. That means the first few hosted responses may be slower until KV warms.
[06:45] Tom: Is there any support for migrating a warm session from on-prem to hosted with state transfer? We could encrypt and transfer just the KV if we strip PHI.
[06:55] Marcus: We have an SDK pattern for state handoff where you can serialize KV, run a client-side filter to remove PHI, and push to hosted warm pool. That requires engineering on your side to ensure redaction. We can help with a small integration project.

[07:15] Rajiv: Ok. Now queueing models — how do you model multi-tier: local GPUs, reserved cloud GPUs, then hosted? We need to know expected waiting time if local is saturated.
[07:27] Marcus: We model it as a tandem queue with finite capacity per tier and priority routing. You can set hard-prefers: local first, then reserved cloud (if not PHI), then hosted. Each tier has its own service rate and warm pool fraction. We compute blocking probabilities using an M/M/c/K approximation for each tier and simulate traces to get percentiles. The simulation results are in the spreadsheet.
[07:50] Sofia: You mentioned K (capacity) — is that the queue length in front of GPUs? We have existing LB queuing with NGINX; how does Redwood's internal queue interact?
[08:00] Marcus: Redwood accepts requests at the gateway and has a short in-memory admission queue per deployment. If the queue exceeds a configured threshold, requests can be redirected, rejected, or throttled. You can also front Redwood with your LB and implement backpressure signals (503/Retry-After). Our recommended pattern: use Redwood's admission control for fine-grained routing and keep your LB for coarse global control.

[08:20] Aisha: On quantization: if you run int8 on hosted and FP16 on-prem, are there output differences? Customers worry about model quality regression.
[08:30] Marcus: There can be subtle differences, yes. We run calibration and A/B quality checks. Redwood Optimize can recommend per-workload quantization profiles and actuate fallbacks: if quality regression goes beyond threshold we can route to higher-precision variant automatically.
[08:45] Sofia: What's the monitoring around that? Who owns the evals?
[08:49] Marcus: You can push prompt-based evals and Redwood will compute quality deltas and alerts. Typically ML team defines the evals; Redwood provides tooling and stores rolling baselines. We'll include an example eval set in the follow-up.

[09:10] Tom: Networking — how do we connect our VPC to Redwood Private control plane? We're behind strict egress policies.
[09:18] Marcus: For Private deployments we offer a customer-managed control plane or a hybrid where you keep data plane private and connect control plane via a narrow egress to Redwood's APIs. We support VPC peering, PrivateLink (cloud-specific), and on-prem connectors over TLS. KMS integration for key exchange is supported (we integrate with AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, and on-prem HSMs).
[09:40] Rajiv: Does that mean audit logs and telemetry can be kept solely in our environment?
[09:43] Marcus: Yes — with Private you can push logs to your SIEM via syslog/ELK/Splunk endpoints; Redwood can ship observability data without payloads. For hosted, we provide audit logs and token-level traces but raw payload storage is optional and can be disabled.

[10:05] Sofia: About warm pool sizing — what's typical for conversational workloads with heavy KV reuse?
[10:12] Marcus: If 70% of session requests are cache hits, you can size warm pools at roughly peak concurrent sessions * average KV working set ratio. Practically, customers start with 20-30% of peak concurrency as warm pool and tune. We also recommend instrumentation: measure cache hit ratio and tail latency during a controlled spike.
[10:30] Aisha: There's also an optimization where you keep trimmed KV: only the last N tokens per session to reduce memory.
[10:36] Marcus: Right, and you can set expiration and LRU policies. Redwood supports per-session TTLs and memory caps.

[10:50] Rajiv: What about fallback models? If our primary LLM is large and we have a spike, can Redwood automatically fall back to a smaller quantized model to meet latency SLOs?
[10:59] Marcus: Yes — the rollout engine supports model variant mapping. You set policy: prefer variant A, if queueing delay > Xms or GPU utilization > Y% switch to variant B. We can also do gradual rollouts and can keep a small percentage on the higher-quality model for accuracy sampling.
[11:18] Sofia: Any gotchas on statefulness when switching variants? Tokenization differences, different vocab or output shape?
[11:24] Marcus: Tokenization usually matches for model families, but if you change architecture or tokenizer there are migration concerns. Best practice is to keep variant family consistent (e.g., same tokenizer, different quant/size). We'll flag migrations in the rollout config.

[11:40] Tom: Circuit breakers — is there automatic suppression if downstream storage is slow and requests pile up?
[11:47] Marcus: Yes, Redwood has circuit-breaker patterns: if KV storage latency or third-party API latency causes per-request service time to exceed thresholds, Redwood can trigger a fast-fail or degrade to stateless mode. You'll configure these thresholds per-route.
[11:59] Rajiv: Could we do a canary where 95% go through normal route and 5% go through a debug path to validate quality during peak?
[12:06] Marcus: Absolutely. A/B and canary is core to our rollout toolset.

[12:20] Sofia: Let's talk numbers for our pilot. We expect baseline average load 350 rps non-PHI, peak bursts up to 1,200 rps short windows. Session reuse expected at 60% KV reuse. Any initial sizing guidance?
[12:34] Marcus: Rough calcs: assume per-GPU throughput 10 rps (given 40 tokens avg and kv hits). For 1,200 rps you'd need ~120 GPUs raw; but with 60% KV reuse effective throughput increases, so maybe ~60-80 GPUs. For pilot, we'd spin up 12-16 GPUs on dedicated reserved and rely on hosted for burst to cover the rest. But I'll compute precise numbers in the sizing spreadsheet.
[12:58] Rajiv: That delta is large; we need cost comparisons — reserved on-prem CAPEX vs hosted per-hour OPEX. Also sequential scale-down implications.
[13:08] Aisha: We'll include that in the model and show break-even points for sustained usage vs spiky.

[13:20] Tom: For the pilot networking, minimal firewall holes — what's required from our side?
[13:26] Marcus: For initial pilot using Redwood Hosted for burst, you'll need outbound TLS to Redwood control plane (port 443) and a small set of IP ranges we'll provide for egress. If you go Private, we do VPC peering or PrivateLink which changes firewall needs.
[13:40] Sofia: And SLA expectations? For dedicated reserved we want 99.9% availability at the region-level.
[13:46] Aisha: Dedicated includes SLA tiers; we'll share the SLA language in the pack. Private deployments can have enterprise SLAs negotiated in the contract.

[13:58] Rajiv: Security review items: SOC2 Type II, ISO 27001, penetration testing cadence, and KMS/HSM options. We'll need the docs.
[14:07] Aisha: We'll send the SOC2 report, the security whitepaper, and the KMS integration guide in the follow-up link.

[14:18] Marcus: Quick note about observability: Redwood Console gives per-token latency histograms, token cost attribution, and per-session traces. For autoscaling we'll expose metrics like queued_ms, active_gpus, kv_hit_rate, and predicted_burst_risk. You can plug them into your Prometheus or use our native dashboards.
[14:38] Tom: Can we emit Redwood metrics to our Grafana? We prefer a single pane.
[14:42] Marcus: Yes, we can forward metrics via Prometheus remote write or push to your Graphite/Grafana stack.

[14:55] Sofia: Testing proposal: start with a 2‑week pilot, generate synthetic traffic modeled on our trace, do a controlled three-day spike window with progressively larger bursts, and evaluate SLOs and cost. Redwood runs the benchmark and we compare.
[15:10] Marcus: Sounds good — I can draft the benchmark plan and acceptance criteria.

[15:20] Rajiv: A couple of smaller Qs — how fast can we add more reserved GPUs? Our procurement lead says adding hardware takes 6–8 weeks.
[15:29] Marcus: For on-prem hardware, obviously procurement delays are typical. That's exactly where burst-to-hosted shines: you avoid overprovisioning while procurement catches up. Also, Redwood Dedicated can provision cloud-reserved capacity faster than buying racks.
[15:43] Tom: Any example customers in regulated health or fintech who've used similar hybrid patterns?
[15:48] Aisha: We have references (non-PHI details) — will include a redacted case study in the follow-up.

[15:58] Sofia: Edge case — what if the hosted region we burst to hits rate limits or capacity constraints? Do you have multi-region fallback?
[16:06] Marcus: Yes, Redwood has smart routing: if a preferred hosted pool is saturated we route to secondary region or degrade to a smaller variant. That's configurable and part of the resilience playbook.

[16:20] Rajiv: Can you walk through a short failure scenario: control plane unreachable but data plane still up? How does private behave?
[16:29] Marcus: For Private, agents run locally and keep serving even if control plane is unreachable for a window. Control plane ops like rollout and config changes will be deferred; metrics may buffer. We have explicit offline modes documented.
[16:45] Tom: So no sudden loss of inference if control plane is down?
[16:49] Marcus: Correct, local data planes keep serving existing models and traffic routing.

[17:00] Aisha: I'm going to propose next steps and action items — quick recap first: Redwood will provide the sizing spreadsheet, security docs, benchmark plan, and a proposed pilot timeline. Marcus will draft a runbook for KV warming and state handoff options. Cobalt to share traffic trace and VPC peering constraints.
[17:20] Rajiv: That's right.

[17:25] Aisha: Ok action items — I'll capture them and send calendar invites for a pilot kickoff the week of Oct 20th.
[17:33] Sofia: That week works.

[17:36] Tom: One last question — the pricing model for hosted burst: is it per-token, per-GPU-hour, or a blended rate?
[17:43] Aisha: For burst we typically bill per-token for hosted inference. For Dedicated we bill reserved GPU capacity monthly. We'll model both in the spreadsheet and show blended cost for your expected mix.
[17:55] Marcus: Also keep in mind that KV cache and batching tweaks can materially change token consumption per user request if you avoid re-sending context.

[18:10] Rajiv: Cool. Thanks everyone. We'll look for the doc pack and the pilot plan.
[18:14] Aisha: Thanks — talk soon.
